title: Chapter 65 – Hu's Left Arm
html:
[Lin Clan – Hu Tieshou]

The granary forge has been cold for six days, and Hu has spent every one of them looking at it.

It is not the cold he minds. A cold forge is a clean thing, an honest thing, like a field after harvest. What he minds is the shape of the quiet. For four months the place has rung from dawn to dark with the sound of Lin hammers and Lin laughter and the long sweet hiss of quench-water. Now the Keepers drill in the quarry, the young refiners have been sent to the Ford to sell, and there is nobody in the building but a one-armed man with a rag in his hand and nine dozen ingots to count.

He counts them. It is not necessary. He does it for the same reason a man touches the hilt of a knife in a crowded street.

Two hundred and sixty days, he thinks, and turns the rag over. Since the last drink.

He has not told anyone he counts. There is nothing to tell. A man who has been drunk for twenty years and stops is not a hero; he is merely a man who has stopped, and the stopping is not a thing you hang on a wall. It is only that the days now have an edge to them, like a blade he must carry in the hand that is not there.

He carries it in the left. The stump is under the sleeve, pinned, a hand's breadth below where the shoulder ends. He has stopped noticing, most days. He notices now, because the door at the back of the forge has opened, and a boy has come in with the snow on his shoulders and a roll of paper under his arm, and he is looking at Hu with the careful face of a man who has rehearsed a speech.

"Do not," says Hu.

"I have not said anything."

"You were going to."

"I was going to ask whether you had eaten."

"I have eaten." He has not. He puts the rag down. "Close the door. It is bad enough that the forge is cold without the wind coming in to look at it."

Jian closes the door. He does it quietly, and bars it, which Hu notices, and files away, as he files away everything that boy does. He stands for a moment with the paper in his hands, in the gray winter light from the high window, and then he says, in a voice that is trying very hard to be a plain one:

"I want to make you an arm."

Hu does not answer.

There is a great deal he could say. He could say that he has been offered an arm before, by a better liar and a worse man, and that he gave it back. He could say that he does not want to be whole. He said it once, under a willow, with a cup of tea going cold in his hand, and meant it more than he has ever meant anything. He could say that a man who has lived twenty years without a limb has earned the right to go on without it, and that the boy should go and find another bone to mend.

He says none of it. He looks at the boy's face, at the narrow, tired, nineteen-year-old face with its gold-ringed eyes, and thinks: He has not slept.

"No," he says.

"I know."

"I am not a thing to be repaired."

"No." Jian does not step back. "I thought of it as a tool. The kind you would want, if you were the one who made them. Not a limb. A tool, built to your specification, to carry a hammer." A pause. "I will not make it if you say no. But I would like you to see it first. The drawing. And tell me what is wrong with it."

It is the last sentence that does it.

Hu has been an artifact refiner for forty years. He has been called a great many things in that time, most of them in a language he would rather forget, but he has never once been asked, by anyone, to find the flaw in a thing before it was built. It is the one request in the world that he cannot refuse. It is the thing his master used to say, in the dark of the Veiled Forge, with a pot of tea and a lamp: Show me the mistake, boy, before the iron does.

He holds out his hand.

* * *

The drawing is not a drawing as the Veiled Forge understood the word.

It is a set of sheets, six of them, with measurements in a neat, narrow script he does not recognize. Not a picture of an arm. A picture of what an arm does. The first sheet shows the shoulder socket, a hollow cup of spirit-iron lined with a sleeve of padded resin, to sit over the stump. The second shows the bones, which are not bones but rods, a main shaft with a hinge at the elbow and a hinge at the wrist. The third is a set of lines and little arrows that Hu stares at for the better part of a quarter hour, until he understands that they are loads. They show where the weight goes when a hammer comes down.

He has drawn the forces, he thinks, with an odd small shock. Like a man who has done it before.

"The elbow is wrong," he says.

"Tell me."

"A single pin. It will shear." He taps the page. "Not on the first swing. On the thousandth. You have given it a pin the size of a thumb and asked it to carry a man's arm and a sixteen-pound hammer. The iron will hold, and the pin will not."

"A double pin?"

"A collar. A sleeve, set over the pin, so the load goes through the sleeve." He takes the brush from the bench and sketches it, on the edge of the sheet, in four quick strokes. "Like that. And turn the main shaft a quarter. You have it running straight. It will fight the wrist."

Jian looks at the sketch for a moment. His mouth moves, soundlessly, as if he were checking a sum.

"It is better," he says. "It is much better." He does not sound embarrassed. He sounds, if anything, a little pleased, in the manner of a man who has been given a gift. "What else?"

They go through all six sheets.

It takes the rest of the afternoon. They stand shoulder to shoulder at the cold bench, Hu with his one hand and Jian with two, and neither of them mentions the thing they are building. They speak of tolerances, and of the heat at which Pool-grade iron will take a quench, and of the sinew. Jian has proposed warden-bark resin for the tendons, which Hu approves of, and a lattice of fine silver wire through the iron to carry Qi, which he does not.

"Silver is soft," he says. "It will drift."

"Not in a lattice. Not if it is laid in a spiral." Jian draws it. "Every turn supports the next."

"Hm." Hu considers this. He has not heard it before. It is not the way a refiner would have done it. It is, he thinks, the way a man would do it who had thought about how things break. "It could work. It would be a nuisance to repair."

"It would not need repair. Not for a long time."

"Everything needs repair."

"Then it would need a little."

He is almost smiling. Hu sees it, and does not remark on it.

When they have finished, the light has gone, and there is a lamp lit on the bench, and the design lies between them, six sheets, covered in two hands. It is a good design. It is better than anything Hu could have drawn alone, and better than anything the boy could have drawn without him. It is, he realizes, a Yellow-grade arm of the high tier, a thing the Veiled Forge would have been proud of in its prime, made with nothing but common iron and a boy's calculation.

And whatever the boy does not say, he thinks.

He has known for a year that there is something behind Lin Jian's eyes. He has known it the way a refiner knows a flaw in a casting: not by looking, but by the sound it makes when struck. He has never asked. A man who has hidden a thing for twenty years does not ask another man what he is hiding.

"I will want the ingots," says Jian. "Mu's. The two from the blade case."

"They are Pool-grade."

"They are the best iron we have."

"They are his." Hu hears the word come out hard. "They were made to hold his blood. I will not put them on my body."

"The blood is not in the iron. I looked." Jian says it steadily. "Whatever he put in that blade, he put in the blade. The ingots are only metal. And you are the one who will decide what metal is."

Hu is silent for a time.

Then he goes to the cabinet at the back of the forge, and takes down a flat box of black lacquer, and sets it on the bench. Inside, wrapped in oiled cloth, are two bars of gray-blue iron, each the length of a forearm. They give off, even through the cloth, a faint cold light. They are the finest metal he has ever held, and the only thing he has taken from Elder Mu's body, and he has not been able to bring himself either to sell them or to melt them down.

"Do what you will," he says.

"Tonight?"

"Tonight." He does not look at the boy. "I will not be in the room."

* * *

He is in the room.

He tells himself he will stand at the far end, by the cold furnace, with his back to the bench. It is a courtesy, to the boy and to himself. He stands there for four breaths. Then he turns round, because a man can only pretend for so long.

The forge is dark except for a single lamp. Jian has laid the ingots on the bench, side by side, with the six sheets of the design weighted flat at the corners. He has taken off his tunic and stands in his under-shirt, thin as a rake, with his sleeves pushed up to the elbow. His eyes are closed. His hands hang a hand's breadth above the iron, palms down, not touching.

Hu has seen a great many things in a forge. He has seen a master pour fire into a mold the color of the sun. He has seen a Rill-stage refiner, at the Sect's own furnace, draw a blade out of a pool of molten stone with a thought. He has seen, once, a thing that he has never described to anyone, in the blackened heart of the Veiled Forge, on the last night.

He has not seen this.

The iron does not melt. It does not glow. It goes quiet, first, as though the air round it had been put under a cloth. Then a thin pale light, not white, not gold, the color a frost makes on a window, begins to run along its edge, the way frost runs along a pane. It does not move quickly. It moves like something being drawn, with great care, by a hand that is not there.

The ingots do not shrink, or fold, or flow. They rearrange. There is no better word. A rod rises from one, smooth and fine as a reed, and lies down on the bench. A collar curls from the end of the second. A thing like a hand-sized cup of gray metal assembles itself from a seam of light, and beside it a chain of small bright links, and a line of silver, no thicker than a hair, which uncoils across the wood in a perfect spiral.

He does not breathe.

Jian's face is wet. Not with tears: with sweat, great clear beads of it, standing on his forehead and running down into the hollows of his eyes. His lips are pressed white. His hands tremble above the iron like a man holding a pot too hot to carry. Hu realizes, with the part of him that is still a refiner and not an old fool, that the boy is paying for this. That every line of silver on the bench is being bought with something, and that the price is not iron.

I should stop him, he thinks.

He does not. He stands in the dark with his one hand pressed flat against his own chest, and watches a child build him an arm out of light.

I will not ask, he thinks. I will not ask. I will not. It is the only prayer he has had in twenty years, and it is not a prayer to anyone.

The light goes out.

It does not fade. It stops, all at once, like a candle pinched between a finger and thumb. In the dark, on the bench, there is a faint metallic ticking as the new metal cools, and the sound of a boy trying to breathe without making any noise at all.

Hu lights the lamp.

The arm lies on the bench, in the yellow light.

It is not beautiful. It is better than that. It is right. A shoulder cup of gray-blue iron, lined with a pad of dark resin; a main shaft that is a little thicker at the elbow, with a collar that he sketched himself, three hours ago, on the corner of a sheet; a hand of five jointed fingers, plain, blunt, each joint a small perfect hinge. It is nearly the color of the stump when it has been cold a day. It gives off no light. It does not hum. It lies there, a little heavy, a little dull, with the faint, cold, ordinary look of a tool that has been made to be used.

Jian is sitting on the floor with his back against the bench and his head tipped back against the wood. His eyes are closed. A thin bright line of red runs from his left nostril to his lip.

"Is it right?" he says, without opening them.

Hu crosses the floor. He kneels, a thing he has not done in years, with a crack in both his knees, and sets his one hand against the boy's chest, to feel for the heartbeat. It is quick, and light, and very steady.

"It is right," he says. His voice is a rasp. "It is the best thing I have ever seen made."

"Good."

"Do not do that again."

"I will not need to." A very faint smile. "It is not a thing I can do for free."

No, thinks Hu. Nothing is.

* * *

It takes three days to fit.

There is no ceremony in it. He is not a man for ceremony. The boy brings the arm in the morning wrapped in a clean cloth, and Hu sits on the anvil stump with his sleeve rolled to the shoulder and says, "Do it," and the boy kneels and seats the cup against the stump with the care of a man setting a bone.

It does not hurt. That is the first surprise. He had expected pain, or at least strangeness, a cold weight on a place that has felt nothing for twenty years. Instead there is a faint, mild pressure, a slow warmth, a sense of something settling into place like a key into a lock. The resin pad takes his heat and shapes itself to the stump. A thread of Qi that he did not send crawls down from his shoulder and into the iron, and is met, on the other side, by the silver spiral.

The fingers move.

They move on their own, first: a twitch, a curl, a slow small opening and closing like a sleeper's hand. Then they move because he asks them. It is not the same as a hand. It is clumsy, a half-beat slow, with none of the feeling of skin. It tells him nothing of heat, or of cold, or of the texture of the cloth. But it closes when he tells it to close, and it opens when he tells it to open, and when he picks up a small hammer from the bench, and closes the iron hand round the haft, and the haft does not slip, he finds that he has stopped breathing.

"It will tire you," says Jian, quietly. He is sitting on his heels a little way off. "It runs on your Qi. A little at rest, more when you push. If you are at full strength for a day, you will be empty by dark. And the resin in the tendons will need renewing every month, or it dries. I wrote it all down."

"Of course you did."

"It will not feel. Not yet. I do not know if it will, in time."

"I did not ask it to."

"No." The boy hesitates. "I am sorry. I could not do better."

Hu looks at the hand. At the five blunt fingers, closed round the haft of a hammer, in the light of a gray winter morning.

"You could not do better," he says, "because there is nothing better to do."

He stands. He walks to the anvil, which has been dead for six days, and lays the cold iron of a half-finished ingot across the horn. He takes the hammer in his right hand, and then, slowly, as if lifting a drowned thing out of water, he takes the haft in both.

Both.

He has not held a hammer in two hands since the night the Veiled Forge burned. He has not had two hands to hold it. He has stood at this anvil, and a hundred others, with a stump pressed against the haft and the haft braced against his hip, and made do. He has made good things, that way. He has made things the Ford buyers called wonders. He has never once made anything that was not a compromise.

He lifts the hammer.

It rises smoothly, with a faint small whisper from the elbow collar. He brings it down.

The ingot rings.

It is a clear, clean, level note, a note he has not heard in twenty years, the sound of a blow that has landed true. It goes through the stone of the floor and up through the soles of his feet. He raises the hammer and strikes again, and again, and again, with the old rhythm, the long slow three-beat that his master taught him: down, turn, down. The iron flattens. The sparks go up in a bright dry rain. He does not stop for a very long time.

When he does, he finds that his face is wet, and that the boy has gone.

He stands in the empty forge with the hammer hanging from his two hands, and the sweat running down his neck, and the cold sun coming through the high window. He does not wipe his eyes. There is no one to see.

It is a decent arm, he thinks, at last.

It is the most he can say. It will have to do.

* * *

The watcher comes on the fourth night, drawn by the heat.

Hu has been expecting him. He has been expecting someone for a month, since the first night he lit the granary furnace after Mu's death and felt, as he stood at the window with the glow of the coals on his face, the small cold prick of an eye on the back of his neck. A forge that burns is a forge that can be seen. It is a lantern on a hill. He has left it burning on purpose.

He sits in the dark of the loft, with the door pulled almost closed, and the new arm lying across his knees like a sleeping dog. He has oiled it. He has tested the grip. He has been practicing, all day, in the empty forge, the slow strange work of making a left hand do what a right hand knows: to lift, to turn, to hold a thing without crushing it. He is clumsy. He is also, he finds, quite a lot stronger than he was.

The watcher comes over the east wall at the second hour after midnight.

He is small, light, and quick, a young man in a gray cloak with a hood pulled low, and he moves like a thing that has been taught to be nothing. He drops to the roof of the shed. He crosses it without a sound. He reaches the high window of the forge, and lies flat, and puts his eye to a crack in the shutter, and watches the red glow of the banked coals.

A Drip, thinks Hu. Third stage. Possibly fourth.

He does not hurry. He has all night. He lets the man watch for a quarter of an hour, and write nothing, and think about whether to go. Then, very softly, he stands, and crosses the loft in his stocking feet, and drops through the hatch behind the man's back like a sack of grain.

The new arm closes round the man's throat.

It does not squeeze. It only holds. But it is iron, and the man, who has been taught everything about hiding and nothing about being held, goes still at once, with a thin sound like a kettle. A knife comes out of his sleeve. Hu catches the wrist with his right hand and twists, once, and the knife falls onto the thatch and slides off the roof.

"Do not," says Hu, in a perfectly gentle voice, "move."

The man does not move.

He is shaking, though. Hu can feel it in the iron, a fine faint tremor, passing up through the silver lattice and into his shoulder like a second pulse. It is a thing he did not expect. He had not thought the arm would feel. It is not a feeling, quite. It is a kind of knowing, as a man in the dark knows a wall is near.

Interesting, he thinks.

"Who sent you?"

"Nobody." The voice is young and hoarse. "I came to see."

"To see what?"

"If it was true. If the old man was dead. If the forge was lit."

"The old man is dead," says Hu. "You may tell him that, if he has a use for it. What did he tell you to do, if you found it lit?"

A silence. Then, very low: "Watch. And count the men."

"And then?"

"And then wait." The man swallows. Hu feels it move against the iron. "There is someone coming. A master. Not a Pool. A Well." The word is a whisper. "The Well-keeper was in the south, at the ford, when Elder Mu died. He is walking. He will be here before the spring. He is..."

He stops.

It is not a hesitation. It is a stop like a man who has run into a wall in the dark, and Hu feels the change in the body in his arms: a sudden terrible stiffening, a long indrawn breath. A thin black line is running up the man's neck, from beneath the collar of his cloak, along the vein, across the jaw, into the ear. It is not a thing that grows. It is a thing that is drawn, by a hand a long way off, with a patient careful pen.

"Wait," says Hu. "Wait. I will not hurt you..."

"It does not matter." The words come out in a hiss, through teeth that have begun to chatter. "It was written when I came. Tell him..." A great shudder. "Tell the boy it is not a master. It is a..."

His eyes roll up. His whole body arches in Hu's grip, and then goes slack.

The black line fades into the skin, as ink fades into water.

Hu stands very still on the roof of the granary, in the cold, with a dead man in his arms and the snow beginning, very softly, to fall.

It is not a master, he thinks. It is a what?

He lays the body down. He closes the eyes with his thumb, as he has done for others, in the years before the drink. He stays there a little while, in the quiet, with the flakes settling on the dead man's hood.

Then he goes down into the forge, and takes from the cabinet a long black bundle wrapped in oiled silk, and carries it out across the yard to the room where a light is still burning.

Jian is awake. He is always awake. He is sitting on the edge of his cot with a book in his lap that he is not reading, and when Hu puts the bundle on the blanket and unwraps it, he looks at it for a long time without touching.

It is a blade. Not long, not ornate: a plain, slightly curved length of gray-blue iron, with a hilt of black leather and a guard of two small bronze lobes. Along the flat, so finely cut that it can only be seen when the light is wrong, run lines of script in a tongue that Hu spent forty years learning and fifteen trying to forget. Coral Gate. It is the key to a door under a hill, and the one piece of Elder Mu's life that the man could not bring himself to leave behind.

"A Well-keeper is coming before the spring," says Hu. "Mu's master's creature. The watcher is dead. He was written to die." He lifts his head. "It will want this. It will want it more than it wants you."

"Then you should keep it," says Jian. "Here. Where it is hidden."

"It is not a thing to hide." Hu pushes the blade across the blanket with two fingers of the iron hand. They do not shake. "It is a key. A key belongs near the door, or in the hand that can use it. I am a man with a new arm and a bad conscience. I will not be the one." He meets the boy's eyes. "You are going where there are a great many doors. Take it. Keep it close. And when the Well-keeper comes, make certain you are not the thing he finds."

Jian looks down at the blade. In the lamplight, the lines of script on the flat seem to shift, very slightly, like a thing breathing.

He puts out his hand, and takes it.
